raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods cross-sectional study in urban Dhaka combines a quantitative matched survey of N = 384 landlord households (192 connected to DWASA foul-water sewers and 192 connected to storm/open drains on the same lanes) with qualitative KIIs (n = 5 DWASA officials), IDIs (n = 10 landlords), and secondary fee schedules. Although the paper reports inferential bivariate statistics (chi-square, t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, and ANOVA with p-values and Cohen's d in Tables 2-4), none of the tested quantitative pairs link a narrow Criterion 2 rule-type legal, tenure, administrative, tariff, or regulatory exposure to a Criterion 4 WASH access outcome. Specifically: (1) 100% of both groups are resident formal house owners/landlords on sewered streets (zero tenure or service-zone variation); (2) quantitative differences test only socio-demographic/housing-age characteristics (e.g., settlement/building duration since construction, p = 0.008), ex-post monthly water/sewer bills resulting from connection ($27 vs $22, p = 0.0002), hypothetical payment motivators, and individual RANAS psychological/attitudinal constructs (perceived health risk, social status, self-efficacy, injunctive norms, and general subjective beliefs about whether cost, awareness, or 'legal issues' obstruct connection [7.3% vs 8.9%, p = 0.574]); and (3) all evidence on narrow Criterion 2 institutional/administrative mechanisms—lengthy DWASA connection approvals (>2 years), DWASA permit/connection fees ($84-$342 USD) versus city corporation drain fees ($41 USD), police fines for unpermitted road-cutting, historical 1990-2000 fee-free connection waves, and DWASA-city corporation coordination failures—is strictly qualitative/descriptive (pp. 10, 12-16).
